authoritativeText.text:
58. What does electrodynamics study?

Mechanics studies the motion of macroscopic objects, meaning objects considered on a scale much larger than individual atoms or molecules.
It relates their motion to the forces acting on them and often treats those forces as known conditions.

Molecular physics studies the thermal motion of atoms and molecules and its connection to heat-related phenomena on a macroscopic scale.
Thermal motion is the microscopic motion associated with temperature.
This comparison does not mean that mechanics and molecular physics never study the origins of interactions.

**Classical electrodynamics studies the properties and laws of electric charges, electric currents, and electromagnetic fields, including electromagnetic interactions and the travel of electromagnetic fields**.
Electric charge is a property of matter.

Charges can be positive or negative, and charged objects can push one another apart or pull one another closer.
Electric current is a flow of charge with an overall direction.

An electromagnetic field has electric and magnetic parts spread through space.
Its electric part can push or pull a charged particle.
Its magnetic part can change the motion of a moving charged particle.

Electromagnetic fields carry energy and momentum, a physical quantity associated with motion.
Charged objects interact with one another through these fields.

An interaction is a way physical objects or particles affect one another.
The fundamental interactions currently known are the gravitational, electromagnetic, strong, and weak interactions①.

Electromagnetic interactions have many different effects in daily life and engineering.
The microscopic basis of elastic forces, friction, and the forces produced by human and other animal muscles mainly involves electromagnetic interactions.
Elastic forces act when a material is deformed, and friction opposes relative sliding or the tendency to slide between surfaces.

The specific behavior of these forces also depends on quantum laws, material structure, or biochemical processes.
Quantum laws govern behavior at the atomic scale, while biochemical processes are chemical processes in living things.
These macroscopic forces cannot simply be equated with the force between two charged particles.

① The weak interaction is involved in certain particle transformations and decays, processes in which particles change into other particles.
Not every particle transformation is caused by the weak interaction.

We can see the words in a book because light, an electromagnetic wave, interacts with matter and our visual system.
An electromagnetic wave is a change in the electric and magnetic parts of a field that travels through space.
The molecular structures and biochemical processes on which life depends also require electromagnetic interactions.

During orbital motion, a spacecraft and the people inside it are usually in approximately free fall, meaning that they fall together under gravity.
The support force, the force that would keep them from falling freely, is very small, so they experience weightlessness.

Weightlessness does not mean that gravity has disappeared: gravity still changes the direction of the spacecraft's motion.
Nor does it mean that long periods of weightlessness have no effect on the human body.

If electromagnetic interactions ceased to exist, existing molecular structures and life processes could not be maintained.
This is a hypothetical situation, not an experiment in which electromagnetic interactions can actually be switched off.

The interaction that plays the main role can differ from one physical system to another.
The scale of a system alone does not establish that a particular interaction is absent.

The nucleus is the small central part of an atom.
It contains protons and usually neutrons.
Protons have positive electric charge, while neutrons have no electric charge.

These particles are called nucleons.
The strong interaction between nucleons plays the main role in holding the nucleus together.
Protons also repel one another through the electromagnetic interaction, which affects the properties of the nucleus.

The arrangement of electrons in atoms, chemical bonds that hold atoms together, and many macroscopic properties of matter mainly involve electromagnetic interactions.
To explain these structures and properties, we also need quantum laws.

Gravity exists between objects with mass at all scales.
It dominates many astronomical systems that, overall, are approximately electrically neutral, meaning that their positive and negative charges nearly balance.

The strong and weak interactions act over very short distances, but weak interactions can have observable effects on a macroscopic scale through processes such as particle decay.
Electromagnetic interactions are therefore involved in many natural phenomena, but they are not the only interaction needed to explain all phenomena.



J. C. Maxwell (1831-1879) was a British physicist and a principal founder of classical electromagnetic field theory.
He developed a unified theory of electricity and magnetism.
Maxwell's equations form the foundation of classical electrodynamics, just as Newton's laws form the foundation of classical mechanics.

Maxwell was also an important founder of the kinetic theory of matter, which describes matter in terms of the motion of its particles.
He used probability, which describes likelihood, and statistical methods, which describe patterns in large groups, to study the motion of many molecules.
These contributions were important to the development of statistical physics, but he should not be described as the first person to use probability and statistics anywhere in physics.

Electrodynamics grew through experiments, theoretical research, and work on new devices.
One early observation was that amber, a hardened tree resin, attracted small, light objects after being rubbed with silk.

Much later, British physicist J. C. Maxwell developed a theory connecting electricity and magnetism.
It included the magnetic effects of changing electric fields.

From his theory, he predicted that electromagnetic waves could travel through space.
Later experiments supported that prediction.
His theory provided an important basis for later radio technology.

Applications of electromagnetic phenomena developed further in the second half of the nineteenth century.
A. C. Popov was an important early participant in radio research and technical development, but radio was established through the work of multiple researchers and practical engineering.

Theory and technology did not always develop in the same order.
Steam engines came before a fully developed theory of heat.

Early electric motors also came before Maxwell's complete electromagnetic field theory.
Early electric motors relied on electromagnetic laws already established by experiment, while radio development was also advanced by the complete field theory and later experiments.
It is therefore incorrect to say that every electromagnetic technology had to wait until the theory was complete.

Widespread applications of electromagnetic phenomena have profoundly changed people's lives.
The generation, transmission, and use of electrical energy, together with electromagnetic technologies such as communication systems, are important foundations of modern society.

Next, we will study electromagnetic interactions.
We will learn the basic laws that describe these interactions.
